arXiv:2504.21015v1 [cs.IR] 20 Apr 2025

Don’t Retrieve, Generate: Prompting LLMs for Synthetic Training Data in Dense Retrieval

Aarush Sinha Affiliation: Chennai, India Email: aarush.sinha@gmail.com
Abstract

Training effective dense retrieval models often relies on hard negative (HN) examples mined from the document corpus via methods like BM25 or cross-encoders (CE), processes that can be computationally demanding and require full corpus access. This paper introduces a different approach, an end-to-end pipeline where a Large Language Model (LLM) first generates a query from a passage, and then generates a hard negative example using only that query text. This corpus-free negative generation contrasts with standard mining techniques. We evaluated this LLM Query →\rightarrow LLM HN approach against traditional LLM Query →\rightarrow BM25 HN and LLM Query →\rightarrow CE HN pipelines using E5-Base and GTE-Base models on several BEIR benchmark datasets. Our results show the proposed all-LLM pipeline achieves performance identical to both the BM25 and the computationally intensive CE baselines across nDCG@10, Precision@10, and Recall@100 metrics. This demonstrates that our corpus-free negative generation method matches the effectiveness of complex, corpus-dependent mining techniques, offering a potentially simpler and more efficient pathway for training high-performance retrievers without sacrificing results. We make the dataset including the queries and the hard-negatives for all three methods publicly available 11 1 https://huggingface.co/collections/chungimungi/arxiv-hard-negatives-68027bbc601ff6cc8eb1f449.

1 Introduction

Dense retrieval models, which encode queries and documents into low-dimensional vectors, are foundational to modern information retrieval systems Karpukhin et al. (2020); Xiong et al. (2020); Reimers and Gurevych (2019). These models typically require fine-tuning on task-specific data using contrastive objectives like triplet loss, which pulls relevant pairs closer while pushing away irrelevant (negative) passages Henderson et al. (2017).

A key factor in effective fine-tuning is the quality of negative examples Xiong et al. (2020). While random negatives are easy to generate, hard negatives semantically related but irrelevant passages provide stronger learning signals Zhan et al. (2021). Traditionally, these are mined from the corpus using methods like BM25 or neural cross-encoders (CEs) for re-ranking Nogueira and Cho (2020); Qu et al. (2021). However, these approaches require access to the full corpus and are resource-intensive, particularly CE-based mining which demands heavy GPU inference and scales poorly with corpus size.

Large Language Models (Brown et al. (2020); Grattafiori et al. (2024); Kavukcuoglu (2025)) have become exceedingly good at understanding and generating text by following user instructions. We propose an alternative, corpus-free pipeline that utilizes the generative abilities of LLMs particularly the Gemini2.5-Pro to generate full training triplets. Our approach includes:

  1. 1.

    Query Generation: Given a positive passage, an LLM generates a corresponding query, similar to prior work like LLM Query.

  2. 2.

    Hard Negative Generation: Conditioned only on the generated query, the LLM produces two semantically challenging but irrelevant passages.

This query-only conditioning for negative generation avoids any corpus lookup or re-ranking, simplifying the pipeline and improving scalability.

We evaluate this end-to-end LLM Query →\rightarrow LLM HN pipeline against two baselines: LLM Query →\rightarrow BM25 HN and LLM Query →\rightarrow CE HN, using E5-Base and GTE-Base models Li et al. (2023) across BEIR datasets Thakur et al. (2021). Notably, our method achieves comparable performance across nDCG@10, Precision@10, and Recall@100, especially with GTE-Base.

In summary, we:

  • •

    Propose a fully LLM-based training data generation pipeline.

  • •

    Introduce a novel query-only, corpus-free hard negative generation method.

  • •

    Demonstrate empirical parity with traditional corpus-mining approaches on BEIR.

  • •

    Highlight significant efficiency and simplicity benefits over existing pipelines.

2 Related Work

Large neural models have been increasingly applied across the information retrieval pipeline. For query understanding, techniques like query expansion or generating hypothetical documents aim to improve retrieval effectiveness Zhu et al. (2023); Ding et al. (2024). Generative models also serve as powerful re-ranking components, refining initial candidate lists through pairwise or listwise comparisons Ma et al. (2023); Qin et al. (2024).

A significant area of research involves using generative models to create synthetic data for training dense retrievers, particularly valuable when labeled data is scarce. Approaches like InPars Bonifacio et al. (2022) generate relevant documents for given queries, while others focus on unsupervised data augmentation Meng et al. (2023) or specialized data for conversational contexts Chen et al. (2024) or training smaller models Tamber et al. (2025).

Most relevant to our work is the exploration of generative models for creating challenging negative samples. SyNeg Wang et al. (2024a), for instance, employs multi-attribute prompting and reflection, often mixing synthetic negatives with traditionally mined ones. Other works optimize training data distributions considering negative samples Ma et al. (2024) or explore negative generation for specific contexts like conversational retrieval Jin et al. (2023). Our approach differs by employing an end-to-end generative pipeline where hard negatives are synthesized conditioned solely on a generated query, explicitly avoiding corpus interaction for negative selection and aiming for performance parity through this simplified process.

3 Methodology

3.1 LLM Prompting

Our approach is straightforward. To construct our corpus, we collect 7,250 abstracts from arXiv across a variety of domains, including mathematics, physics, computer science, and others. We utilize the Gemini 2.5 (Pro -03-25) via Google AI Studio22 2 https://aistudio.google.com. A detailed usage of the resources required for all methods used is provided in Table 5 of Appendix C.

To generate queries, we provide the model with a system instruction: For each abstract generate a 20 word query, followed by the respective abstract from our corpus. We set the temperature to 0.3 and top-p to 95 for generating queries. Before prompting the model to generate hard negatives, we first ask it to define the term hard negative in the context of information retrieval. The exact response of the model is seen in Figure 2 in Appendix A, and is used as the basis for the generating the hard negatives of synthetic corpus free, as seen in Figure 1. Using only the query, we prompt the model to generate two passages that serve as hard negatives. Each passage is constrained to 75 to 100 words, in accordance with the typical length of an abstract. We set the temperature to 0.5 and top-p to 95 for generating that hard negatives. This is the exact prompt we gave the LLM: Generate 2 passages for each query. Ensure that the passages are hard negatives in terms of information retrieval. The passage should be max of 100 words but no less than 75.

This entire process approximately took no more than 10 minutes. We also provide examples of the responses of the LLM for both the query and hard negatives in Table 2 of Appendix B.

3.2 Traditional/Baseline Methods

For our baseline methods, we use the same queries generated by the LLM. We follow standard retrieval setups for both the BM25 and cross-encoder approaches, retrieving the top 50 hard negatives in each case. For cross encoder baselines, we utilize msmarco-distilbert-base-v3 and all-MiniLM-L6-v3 from the sentence-transformers library Reimers and Gurevych (2019).

All experiments were performed on an NVIDIA V100 GPU (32GB). The entire process from query generation to hard negative retrieval takes approximately 30 minutes. We also provide the query generated by LLM Query 33 3 LLM Query refers to queries generated by the LLM from the positive passage, and this method is used for query generation across all compared pipelines and the retrieved hard-negatives for both the BM25 and cross-encoder mining methods in Tables 3 and Table 4 respectively of Appendix B.

4 Fine Tuning

We fine-tune both E5-Base Wang et al. (2024b) and GTE-Base Li et al. (2023) for 25 steps using the queries and corresponding hard negatives across all three configurations with a batch_size of 16. Optimization is performed using the triplet loss:

ℒtriplet=max⁡(0,d⁡(f⁡(q),f⁡(p))−d⁡(f⁡(q),f⁡(n))+α)\mathcal{L}_{\text{triplet}}=\max\left(0,\,d(f(q),f(p))-d(f(q),f(n))+\alpha\right) (1)

Fine-tuning is executed on a single V100 GPU (32GB), completing in under one minute. We start seeing drops in retrieval performance after 25 steps of fine tuning as seen in Appendix D.

5 Results

We evaluated our proposed end-to-end generative pipeline (LLM Query + LLM HN), using an LLM for both query generation and corpus-free hard negative generation. This was compared against baselines using the same LLM queries but with BM25-mined (LLM Query + BM25 HN) or cross-encoder-mined (LLM Query + CE HN) hard negatives. Evaluations employed E5-Base and GTE-Base models on 10 BEIR datasets, measuring nDCG@10, Precision@10 (P@10), and Recall@100.

Detailed results are presented in Table 1. The primary finding concerns the GTE-Base model: our proposed pipeline (LLM Query + LLM HN) achieved performance virtually identical to both the BM25 HN and CE HN baselines across all datasets and metrics (e.g., average nDCG@10: 0.495 for all methods, with negligible differences in the 4th decimal place for CE HN averages). For E5-Base, performance was also highly similar across the three methods (average nDCG@10: 0.441 for all). Minor differences (e.g., 0.001 nDCG@10 on COVID) were observed between our method and the baselines on individual datasets, but overall parity was maintained. As expected, GTE-Base consistently outperformed E5-Base (e.g., average nDCG@10 0.495 vs 0.441).

This performance parity, especially for GTE-Base, suggests that all three negative generation strategies may provide a sufficiently strong training signal for the models to approach their performance ceiling on these benchmarks and metrics. Therefore, our corpus-free negative generation approach demonstrates effectiveness comparable to established, computationally intensive corpus-dependent mining techniques in this experimental setup.

6 Conclusion

We presented an end-to-end pipeline using Large Language Models to generate queries and corresponding hard negatives conditioned solely on the query text, bypassing corpus mining for negatives. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach achieves retrieval performance identical to strong baselines using traditional BM25 or cross-encoder negative mining, particularly with the GTE-Base model across several benchmarks (nDCG@10, P@10, R@100).

This performance parity highlights the potential of our method to significantly simplify the training pipeline and reduce computational overhead associated with corpus indexing or re-ranking, without sacrificing retrieval effectiveness. Our corpus-free negative generation strategy offers a viable and efficient alternative for training dense retrievers, especially valuable when corpus access or mining resources are limited. Future work could explore generalization across different models, generative sources, and dataset types.

7 Future Work

Our future research involves extending the evaluation framework considerably. We aim to assess the adaptability of our method by applying it to a wider spectrum of Large Language Models, exemplified by models like Claude and the GPT family. A parallel and crucial objective is to test its robustness and scalability more thoroughly by utilizing a significantly larger text corpus, ensuring its efficacy under increased data volume and complexity.

8 Limitation

Our experiments were conducted using specific dense retriever architectures (E5-Base and GTE-Base). The performance equivalence observed might not directly generalize to significantly larger or different types of retrieval models without further investigation. Another limitation is our corpus being only 7250 abstracts. This relatively small and domain-specific initial set for query generation might limit the generalization of our findings, as the resulting synthetic training data may not fully reflect the challenges present when training or evaluating retrievers on much larger and more varied corpora. Dependency on a specific, experimental version of Gemini 2.5 (Pro -03-25) limits the study, as future model updates could alter generative behavior, while discontinuation would impede reproducibility.

Appendix A What is a Hard Negative according to Gemini2.5-Pro ?

To ensure the Large Language Model understood the specific requirements for generating hard negatives relevant to information retrieval, we first prompted Gemini 2.5 Pro for a definition. This initial step helped ground the subsequent generation task. Figure 2 below presents the verbatim response received from the model, outlining its understanding of hard negatives, including their types, importance, and common mining techniques. This definition formed the conceptual basis used when prompting the model to generate the actual hard negative examples for our experiments, as described in Section 3.1.

Appendix B Comparison of Generated Queries and Retrieved/Generated Hard Negatives

To provide a qualitative illustration of the different data generation pipelines, this section presents concrete examples derived from the same source passage. Table 2 shows the query and the corresponding hard negative generated entirely by our proposed LLM-based method. Table 3 shows the query generated by the LLM Query model and a hard negative retrieved for that query using BM25 mining. Finally, Table 4 shows the LLM Query query paired with a hard negative identified via cross-encoder re-ranking. These examples allow for a direct comparison of the query styles and the nature of the hard negatives produced by each distinct approach.

To provide further insight into the characteristics of the training data components produced by each pipeline, Figure 3 visualizes the semantic relationships. Cosine similarities were computed using the sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2 representation model, comparing the query, the original passage, and the corresponding hard negative example for each of the three methods.

Several observations emerge from this comparison. Firstly, the similarity between the query and the source passage (blue bars) differs depending on the query generation technique, reflecting the distinct nature of the queries produced by our generative approach versus LLM Query. Secondly, the Query vs. Hard Negative similarities (orange bars) indicate that all three methods successfully identify or create negative examples that possess considerable semantic closeness to the query, confirming their status as challenging distractors rather than simple, easily distinguishable negatives.

The most significant distinction, however, lies in the Passage vs. Hard Negative similarities (grey bars). The negative example produced by our synthetic generation method exhibits markedly lower similarity to the original source passage compared to the negatives retrieved from the document collection via BM25 or cross-encoder re-ranking. The BM25-retrieved negative, in particular, displays a very high degree of similarity to the source passage, likely indicating significant lexical or fine-grained topical overlap found within the corpus. In contrast, the synthetically generated negative, while semantically related to the query, is considerably less similar to the specific content of the original passage.

This pattern strongly corroborates the design of our proposed method, where negative examples are constructed based solely on the query text, independent of the original passage content. It highlights a fundamental difference in the nature of the negative examples used for training: while the corpus-mining approaches find existing documents that closely resemble the positive passage, our approach generates novel distractors focused on query relevance. This analysis underscores that although the different pipelines yield equivalent final retrieval performance (as shown in Section 5), the underlying training data possesses demonstrably distinct characteristics, reinforcing the viability of achieving strong results without direct corpus interaction during negative selection.

Appendix C Resource Usage

Beyond retrieval effectiveness, the practical viability of a training pipeline depends significantly on its resource requirements. Table 5 provides a comparative summary of the approximate resource usage for the data preparation and fine-tuning stages associated with our proposed method and the baseline approaches. The table details the primary hardware utilized, approximate GPU VRAM consumption for relevant components, estimated wall-clock time for processing the full dataset, and the associated cost profile, highlighting the potential efficiency benefits of the generative approach.

Appendix D Impact of Fine-Tuning Steps

To understand the effect of fine-tuning duration on retrieval performance and further validate our findings, we conducted an ablation study varying the number of fine-tuning steps. This analysis focuses on the GTE-Base model, evaluating its performance when trained using the three different hard negative generation strategies: our proposed corpus-free LLMQuery+LLM-HN, the cross-encoder mined LLMQuery+CN-HN, and the BM25 mined LLMQuery+BM25-HN.

We tracked the average performance across six diverse BEIR datasets (NFCorpus, SciFact, Scidocs, Arguana, FIQA, and Touche2020) for key retrieval metrics: nDCG@10, Precision@10 (P@10), and Recall@100. The results are visualized in Figures 4, 5, and 6, plotting the respective average metric scores against the number of fine-tuning steps from 0 up to approximately 250.

Observations:

  1. 1.

    nDCG@10 (Figure 4): Average nDCG@10 improves significantly within the initial fine-tuning steps (roughly up to 25 steps). However, beyond this initial peak, we observe a trend where performance plateaus and can even slightly decrease with further fine-tuning. This pattern of diminishing returns or slight degradation is consistent across all three hard negative generation methods (LLM-HN, CN-HN, and BM25-HN). This observation supports our decision to fine-tune for only 25 steps in the main experiments (Table 1), as this duration captures the substantial initial performance gains while avoiding potential degradation from excessive fine-tuning. Importantly, even at 25 steps, the performance parity between our proposed method and the baselines is clearly evident.

  2. 2.

    Precision@10 (Figure 5): Average P@10 increases sharply in the early stages of fine-tuning (up to  50 steps). All three hard negative strategies yield nearly identical P@10 performance after this initial convergence. There is a slight peak followed by a gentle decrease in performance as fine-tuning progresses further for all methods.

  3. 3.

    Recall@100 (Figure 6): The average Recall@100 metric exhibits a slightly different trend. Performance generally increases steadily for LLM-HN and CN-HN across the observed range, suggesting potential for minor further gains with extended fine-tuning for this specific metric. The BM25-HN method shows a similar increasing trend but remains slightly below the other two. Critically, the performance gap between our proposed LLM-HN and the computationally intensive CN-HN remains negligible across all steps.

This ablation study reinforces the central claim of our paper. The performance parity observed between our corpus-free LLMQuery+LLM-HN method and the traditional corpus-dependent LLMQuery+BM25-HN and LLMQuery+CN-HN methods is robust across different fine-tuning durations, especially after the initial convergence phase.
